# canonical models {.divider}

$\Sigma$ **characterizes** a class of frames $\mathcal{C}$ iff $\Sigma$ is sound and complete with respect to $\mathcal{C}$:
$$\vdash_\Sigma \varphi \quad \text{iff} \quad \models_{\mathcal{C}} \varphi$$

## how to justify each direction ($\Rightarrow$)

$\Sigma$ is sound with respect to $\mathcal{C}$:

$$\vdash_\Sigma \varphi \quad \text{only if} \quad \models_{\mathcal{C}} \varphi$$

::: {.incremental}
- We argue that the axioms of $\Sigma$ are valid in all frames in $\mathcal{C}$.

- We observe that both $\textsf{MP}$ and $\textsf{RN}$ preserve validity in all frames in $\mathcal{C}$.
:::


## how to justify each direction ($\Leftarrow$)

$\Sigma$ is complete with respect to $\mathcal{C}$:

$$\vdash_\Sigma \varphi \quad \text{if} \quad \models_{\mathcal{C}} \varphi$$

We argue by contraposition. If $\nvdash_\Sigma \varphi$, then $\varphi$ is not valid in all frames in $\mathcal{C}$. That is, if $\nvdash_\Sigma \varphi$, then we find a world at which $\varphi$ fails in *some model based on* a frame in $\mathcal{C}$.

::: {.incremental}
- We build the **canonical model** $\mathcal{M}_\Sigma$ for $\Sigma$ from maximal $\Sigma$-consistent sets of formulas.

- We verify that the canonical for $\Sigma$ is a member of the class $\mathcal{C}$.
:::


## the strategy

![](images/strategy.svg){.nostretch width="90%" fig-align="center"}

. . .

Each arrow will be justified in this deck:

- Theorem 8.1, 
- Lindenbaum's Lemma,
- Truth Lemma.

# consistency {.divider}

## derivability

::: {.definition}
$\varphi$ is **$\Sigma$-derivable** from $\Gamma$, written $\Gamma \vdash_\Sigma \varphi$, iff there is a finite conjunction $\boldsymbol{\alpha}$ of formulas $\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n \in \Gamma$ for which
$$\vdash_\Sigma \boldsymbol{\alpha} \to \varphi$$
:::

. . .

We do *not* allow premises *inside* a derivation. Otherwise, $\textsf{RN}$ would yield $p \vdash_\Sigma \Box p$, which is undesirable.

## consistency

::: {.definition}
$\Gamma$ is **$\Sigma$-consistent** iff $\Gamma \nvdash_\Sigma \bot$. That is, there is no finite conjunction $\boldsymbol{\alpha}$ of members of $\Gamma$ for which
$$\vdash_\Sigma \boldsymbol{\alpha} \to \bot$$
:::

. . .

Otherwise, $\Gamma$ is **$\Sigma$-inconsistent**.

$\varphi$ is $\Sigma$-consistent iff $\{\varphi\}$ is. That is, $\varphi$ is $\Sigma$-consistent iff $\nvdash_\Sigma \varphi \to \bot$. 



## derivability and inconsistency

::: {.theorem}
$\Gamma \vdash_\Sigma \varphi$ iff $\Gamma, \neg \varphi$ is $\Sigma$-inconsistent.
:::

::: {.proof}
We consider each direction in turn:

($\Rightarrow$) Given a finite conjunction $\boldsymbol{\alpha}$ of members of $\Gamma$, if $\vdash_\Sigma \boldsymbol{\alpha} \to \varphi$, then $\vdash_\Sigma (\boldsymbol{\alpha} \wedge \neg \varphi) \to \varphi$, and, by $\textsf{PL}$, $\vdash_\Sigma (\boldsymbol{\alpha} \wedge \neg \varphi) \to \bot$. Therefore, $\Gamma, \neg\varphi$ is $\Sigma$-inconsistent.

($\Leftarrow$) Suppose $\vdash_\Sigma (\boldsymbol{\alpha} \wedge \neg \varphi) \to \bot$ for some conjunction $\boldsymbol{\alpha}$ of members of $\Gamma$. Since $\vdash_\Sigma \neg \bot$, we have $\vdash_\Sigma \neg(\boldsymbol{\alpha} \wedge \neg \varphi)$, whence $\vdash_\Sigma \boldsymbol{\alpha} \to \varphi$ by $\textsf{PL}$. Thus $\Gamma \vdash_\Sigma \varphi$.
:::

In particular, $\nvdash_\Sigma \varphi$ iff $\neg \varphi$ is $\Sigma$-consistent.

# maximal consistency {.divider}

## maximal $\Sigma$-consistent sets {.smaller}

::: {.definition}
$\Gamma$ is **maximal $\Sigma$-consistent** iff

1. $\Gamma$ is $\Sigma$-consistent, and
2. for each $\varphi$, if $\Gamma, \varphi$ is $\Sigma$-consistent, then $\varphi \in \Gamma$.
:::

. . .

::: {.theorem}
(**Lindenbaum theorem**) If $\Delta$ is $\Sigma$-consistent set, then $\Delta$ is a subset of some maximal $\Sigma$-consistent set $\Gamma$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Enumerate all the formulas of propositional logic 

$$
\varphi_0, \varphi_1, \varphi_2, \dots
$$ 
and build a chain

$$
\Gamma = \Sigma_0 \subseteq \Sigma_1 \subseteq \Sigma_2 \subseteq \cdots
$$
where $\Sigma_{0}$ is $\Gamma$ and $\Sigma_{n+1}$ is $\Sigma_n, \varphi_n$ if that set is *consistent*, and $\Sigma_n$ otherwise. 

Let $\Sigma = \bigcup_n \Sigma_n$. Notice that the identity of $\Sigma$ is very sensitive to the details of the enumeration. 
:::



## a maximal consistent set as a world

![](images/mcs.svg){.nostretch width="72%" fig-align="center"}

A maximal $\Sigma$-consistent set gives a complete and consistent description of a way the world might be. These will be the worlds of the canonical model for $\Sigma$.

## maximal consistent sets {.smaller}

::: {.theorem}
If $\Gamma$ is maximal $\Sigma$-consistent, then

$$
\begin{array}{llll}
1. & \Gamma \vdash_\Sigma \varphi & \text{iff} & \varphi \in \Gamma \\
2. & \neg \varphi \in \Gamma & \text{iff} & \varphi \notin \Gamma\\
3. & \varphi \to \psi \in \Gamma & \text{iff} & \varphi \notin \Gamma \ \text{or} \ \psi \in \Gamma \\
\end{array}
$$
:::

::: {.proof}
We look at each case in turn:

1. $\Gamma \vdash_\Sigma \varphi \Leftrightarrow \varphi \in \Gamma$

($\Rightarrow$) If $\Gamma \vdash_\Sigma \varphi$, then $\Gamma, \neg\varphi$ is $\Sigma$-inconsistent. If $\varphi \notin \Gamma$, then, by maximal $\Sigma$-consistency, $\Gamma, \varphi$ is $\Sigma$-inconsistent. But if both $\Gamma, \varphi$ and $\Gamma, \neg \varphi$ are $\Sigma$-inconsistent, $\Gamma$ alone must be, contrary to assumption.

  ($\Leftarrow$) Since $\vdash_\Sigma \varphi \to \varphi$.

2. $\neg \varphi \in \Gamma \Leftrightarrow \varphi \notin \Gamma$

    ($\Rightarrow$) If $\neg \varphi \in \Gamma$, then $\Gamma \vdash_\Sigma \neg\varphi$, so $\varphi \notin \Gamma$ by consistency. 

    ($\Leftarrow$) If $\varphi \notin \Gamma$, then $\Gamma, \neg\neg\varphi$ is $\Sigma$-inconsistent, and thus $\Gamma \vdash_\Sigma \neg \varphi$ by Theorem 8.1.

:::

# accessibility {.divider}

## the canonical accessibility relation

::: {.definition}
For maximal $\Sigma$-consistent $\Gamma, \Delta$:
$$\Gamma R \Delta \quad \text{iff} \quad \{\varphi : \Box \varphi \in \Gamma\} \subseteq \Delta$$
:::

![](images/acc-box.svg){.nostretch width="62%" fig-align="center"}

## an equivalent characterization

::: {.theorem}
$\{\Diamond \varphi : \varphi \in \Delta\} \subseteq \Gamma$ iff $\{\varphi : \Box \varphi \in \Gamma\} \subseteq \Delta$
:::

![](images/acc-dia.svg){.nostretch width="62%" fig-align="center"}

## proof

::: {.theorem}
$\{\Diamond \varphi : \varphi \in \Delta\} \subseteq \Gamma$ iff $\{\varphi : \Box \varphi \in \Gamma\} \subseteq \Delta$
:::

::: {.proof}
We look at each direction in turn:

($\Rightarrow$) Suppose $\{\Diamond \varphi : \varphi \in \Delta\} \subseteq \Gamma$ and $\Box \varphi \in \Gamma$. For reductio, suppose $\varphi \notin \Delta$. Then $\neg \varphi \in \Delta$, so $\Diamond \neg \varphi \in \Gamma$, i.e., $\neg \Box \neg\neg \varphi \in \Gamma$. Since $\vdash_\Sigma \neg \Box \neg \neg \varphi \leftrightarrow \neg \Box \varphi$, we get $\neg \Box \varphi \in \Gamma$, and so $\Box \varphi \notin \Gamma$. Contradiction.

($\Leftarrow$) Suppose $\{\varphi : \Box \varphi \in \Gamma\} \subseteq \Delta$. We now argue for the conditional: if $\Diamond \varphi \notin \Gamma$, then $\varphi \notin \Delta$. If $\neg \Box \neg \varphi \notin \Gamma$, then $\Box \neg \varphi \in \Gamma$ by maximality. So $\neg \varphi \in \Delta$, and $\varphi \notin \Delta$.
:::

## $\Diamond$ and $\Box$ in maximal consistent sets {.smaller}

::: {.theorem}
If $\Gamma$ is maximal $\Sigma$-consistent, then

$$
\begin{array}{llll}
\text{a.} & \Diamond \varphi \in \Gamma & \text{iff} & \text{for some max $\Sigma$-con} \ \Delta, \ \Gamma R \Delta \ \text{and} \ \varphi \in \Delta\\
\text{b.} & \Box \varphi \in \Gamma & \text{iff} & \text{for every max $\Sigma$-con} \ \Delta, \ \text{if} \ \Gamma R \Delta, \ \text{then} \ \varphi \in \Delta
\end{array}
$$
:::

. . .

Part (b) will follow from (a) by duality.

Focus on (a) for now: 

- $(\Leftarrow)$ is immediate from the definition of $R$.

- $(\Rightarrow)$ is the **existence lemma**.

## the existence lemma {.smaller}

**Plan**. If $\Diamond \varphi \in \Gamma$, we set out *build* an accessible $\Delta$ that contains $\varphi$. We need only check that the following set is $\Sigma$-consistent:

$$
\{\varphi\} \cup \{\psi : \Box\psi \in \Gamma\}
$$

![](images/existence.svg){.nostretch width="60%" fig-align="center"}

If a maximal $\Sigma$-consistent set $\Delta$ extends $\{\psi : \Box \psi \in \Gamma\}$, then it is accessible from $\Gamma$. 

## proof {.smaller}

::: {.theorem}
If $\Gamma$ is maximal $\Sigma$-consistent and $\Diamond \varphi \in \Gamma$, then $\{\varphi\} \cup \{\psi : \Box\psi \in \Gamma\}$ is $\Sigma$-consistent.
:::

::: {.proof}
Suppose not. Then for some $\Box\psi_1, \dots, \Box\psi_n \in \Gamma$:

$$
\begin{array}{lll}
1 & \vdash_\Sigma \varphi \wedge (\psi_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \psi_n) \to \bot & \\
2 & \vdash_\Sigma (\psi_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \psi_n) \to \neg \varphi & \textsf{PL} \ 1\\
3 & \vdash_\Sigma (\Box\psi_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \Box\psi_n) \to \Box \neg \varphi & \text{normality} \ 2\\
4 & (\Box\psi_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \Box\psi_n) \to \Box \neg \varphi \in \Gamma & \Gamma \ \text{contains theorems}\\
5 & \Box\psi_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \Box\psi_n \in \Gamma & \text{closure}\\
6 & \Box \neg \varphi \in \Gamma & 4, 5
\end{array}
$$

But $\Box \neg \varphi$ is equivalent to $\neg \Diamond \varphi$, which contradicts $\Diamond \varphi \in \Gamma$ given the $\Sigma$-consistency of $\Gamma$. So the set is $\Sigma$-consistent.
:::
By Lindenbaum lemma, we may extends the set to the required $\Delta$.

# the canonical model {.divider}

## definition {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.definition} 
The **canonical model** $\mathcal{M}_\Sigma = (W_\Sigma, R_\Sigma, V_\Sigma)$ for $\Sigma$:

1. $W_\Sigma$ is the set of all maximal $\Sigma$-consistent sets.
2. $\Gamma R_\Sigma \Delta$ iff $\{\Diamond \varphi : \varphi \in \Delta\} \subseteq \Gamma$. That is, iff $\{\varphi : \Box \varphi \in \Gamma\} \subseteq \Delta$.
3. $V_\Sigma(p) = \{\Gamma \in W_\Sigma : p \in \Gamma\}$.
:::

::: {style="height: 20px;"}
:::

The **canonical frame** for $\Sigma$ is $(W_\Sigma, R_\Sigma)$.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](images/canon.svg){.nostretch width="120%" fig-align="center"}
:::
:::



## the truth lemma {.smaller}

::: {.theorem}
For each maximal $\Sigma$-consistent set $\Gamma$ and each $\varphi$:
$$\mathcal{M}_\Sigma, \Gamma \Vdash \varphi \quad \text{iff} \quad \varphi \in \Gamma$$
:::

::: {.proof}
By induction on the complexity of $\varphi$:
$$
\begin{array}{lllll}
\text{Base case}: & & & & \\
&\mathcal{M}_\Sigma, \Gamma \Vdash p & \text{iff } & \Gamma \in V_\Sigma(p) & \\
& & \text{iff } & p \in \Sigma & \textsf{definition of} \ \Vdash \\[8pt]
\text{Induction step for }  \neg\textbf{:} & & & & \\
& \mathcal{M}_\Sigma, \Gamma \Vdash \neg \varphi & \text{iff } & \mathcal{M}_\Sigma, \Gamma \nVdash \varphi & \textsf{definition of} \ \Vdash \\
& & \text{iff } & \varphi \notin \Sigma & \textsf{inductive hypothesis} \\
& & \text{iff } & \neg \varphi \in \Sigma & \textsf{maximal consistency} \\[8pt]
\text{Induction step for } \to\textbf{:} & & & & \\
& \mathcal{M}_\Sigma, \Gamma \Vdash \varphi \to \psi & \text{iff } & \mathcal{M}_\Sigma, \Gamma \nVdash \varphi \text{or} \ \mathcal{M}_\Sigma, \Gamma \Vdash \psi & \textsf{definition of} \ \Vdash \\
& & \text{iff } & \varphi \notin \Sigma \ \text{or} \ \psi \in \Sigma & \textsf{inductive hypothesis} \\
& & \text{iff } & \varphi \to \psi \in \Sigma & \textsf{maximal consistency} \\
\end{array}
$$
:::

## truth lemma: $\Box$ {.smaller}

::: {.proof}
$$
\begin{array}{lllll}
& \mathcal{M}_\Sigma, \Gamma \Vdash \Box \varphi & \text{iff } & \text{for all} \ \Delta \in W_\Sigma, \ \text{if} \ \Gamma R_\Sigma \Delta, \ \text{then} \ \mathcal{M}_\Sigma, \Delta \Vdash \varphi & \textsf{definition of} \ \Vdash \\
&           & \text{iff} & \text{for all} \ \Delta \in W_\Sigma, \ \text{if} \ \Gamma R_\Sigma \Delta, \ \text{then} \ \varphi \in \Delta & \textsf{inductive hypothesis}\\
&           & \text{iff} & \Box \varphi \in \Gamma  & \textsf{Thm 8.4b}\\
\end{array}
$$
:::

![](images/truth-box.svg){.nostretch width="52%" fig-align="center"}

This is the only step where the existence lemma is needed.


## where we stand

![](images/strategy.svg){.nostretch width="85%" fig-align="center"}

::: {.incremental}
- If $\nvdash_\Sigma \varphi$, then $\varphi$ fails at some world of $\mathcal{M}_\Sigma$.

- So $\Sigma$ is complete with respect to a class of frames $\mathcal{C}$ if $\mathcal{C}$ contains the canonical frame for $\Sigma$.
:::

## corollary: $\textsf{K}$ is complete with respect to all frames

::: {.theorem}
$\textsf{K}$ is complete with respect to the class of *all* frames.
:::

::: {.proof}
The canonical frame for $\textsf{K}$, $(W_\textsf{K}, W_\textsf{K})$, belongs to the class of all frames.
:::
